Clock Problems.title: ⏰ Clock Problems — Complete Theory
Clock Problems.overview: Clock aptitude problems study the relative motion of the hour, minute and second hands. The key idea is that the hour hand does not stay fixed: it moves 0.5° every minute. Most questions reduce to angular position, relative speed, or time-rate conversion.
concepts: A complete analog clock is 360° and has 12 hour marks, so adjacent hour marks are 30° apart.
The minute hand completes 360° in 60 minutes: 6° per minute.
The hour hand completes 360° in 12 hours: 30° per hour or 0.5° per minute.
The second hand moves 6° per second.
The relative speed of minute hand with respect to hour hand is 6 − 0.5 = 5.5° per minute.
formulas: For coincidence in the H-th hour: M = 60H/11 minutes
Mirror time = 11:60 − actual time for a 12-hour analog clock
examples: Minute hand = 150°. Hour hand = 210 + 12.5 = 222.5°. Smaller angle = 72.5°.
mistakes: Using 30H − 6M ignores hour-hand movement.
Forgetting to choose the smaller angle when asked for the angle between hands.
Treating 12 as H=12 instead of H=0 in the angle formula.
Using a fast/slow clock rate without distinguishing displayed elapsed time from real elapsed time.
tips: For coincidence/opposite/right-angle questions, use relative motion rather than guessing.
Keep fractional minutes until the final step when exactness matters.

Calendar Problems.title: 📅 Calendar Problems — Complete Theory
Calendar Problems.overview: Calendar aptitude problems are based on the seven-day cycle, month lengths, leap-year rules, odd days, date differences, and modular arithmetic. The safest approach is to reduce total day counts modulo 7.
concepts: A normal Gregorian year has 365 days = 52 weeks + 1 odd day.
A leap year has 366 days = 52 weeks + 2 odd days.
Gregorian leap year rule: divisible by 4, except century years unless divisible by 400.
A 400-year Gregorian cycle contains exactly 146097 days = 20871 weeks, so the calendar repeats after 400 years.
formulas: Day shift after N days = N mod 7
Leap year: divisible by 4 and (not divisible by 100 or divisible by 400)
Date difference = sum of remaining days in the first month + complete middle months + days in final month, or use direct date arithmetic
Same calendar requires matching weekday pattern and the same leap/non-leap month structure
examples: It was Friday in the Gregorian calendar.
100 mod 7 = 2, so the weekday shifts forward by 2 days.
1900 is not a leap year because it is a century not divisible by 400; 2000 is a leap year because 2000 is divisible by 400.
mistakes: Treating every year divisible by 4 as leap without checking century rules.
Counting both endpoints when a question asks for elapsed days between dates.
Forgetting that February has 29 days in a leap year.
Forgetting to reduce large day counts modulo 7.
tips: Write the leap-year rule explicitly before solving century questions.
For weekday shifts, use N mod 7 immediately.
For same-calendar questions, check both weekday alignment and leap/non-leap status.

Pattern Recognition.title: 🔢 Pattern Recognition — Complete Theory
Pattern Recognition.overview: Pattern questions ask you to infer a consistent rule from a sequence, figure, or relationship. Start with the simplest transformations before testing more complex ones.
concepts: First differences: subtract consecutive terms.
Second differences: compare consecutive differences when the first differences are not constant.
Ratios: divide a term by the previous term when multiplication is likely.
Alternating patterns: odd and even positions may follow different rules.
Mixed operations can combine multiplication/addition or subtraction/division.
formulas: Quadratic sequences often have constant second differences
examples: Differences are 3, 5, 7, so the next difference is 9 and the answer is 26.
mistakes: Choosing a complicated rule when a simpler consistent rule exists.
Checking only one transition instead of the entire sequence.
tips: Test differences, ratios, alternation, and known number families in that order.

Tabular Data Interpretation.title: 📊 Tabular Data Interpretation — Complete Theory
Tabular Data Interpretation.overview: Tabular DI converts rows and columns into numerical comparisons. Read labels and units first, then calculate totals, averages, differences, ratios, and percentage changes.
concepts: Identify row categories, column headings, units, and time periods.
Totals are found by summing the relevant cells.
An average is total divided by the number of observations.
Percentage change compares a new value with the original value.
Ratios should be simplified when appropriate.
formulas: Ratio A:B = A/B and can be reduced by a common factor
mistakes: Using the new value as the denominator for percentage change.
Mixing units or comparing percentages with raw values.
tips: Underline the exact row/column named in the question before calculating.

Bar Graph Analysis.title: 📈 Bar Graph Analysis — Complete Theory
Bar Graph Analysis.overview: Bar graphs compare discrete categories using bar height or length. Questions commonly ask for highest/lowest values, differences, totals, ratios, and percentage changes.
concepts: Read the axis scale before reading a bar value.
Compare bars directly for highest, lowest, and ranking questions.
For totals, add the values represented by the relevant bars.
For percentage change, use the original value as the denominator.
formulas: Percentage increase = (A−B)/B × 100 when B is the original value
mistakes: Misreading the graph scale.
Comparing visual bar lengths without reading numeric labels.
tips: Always inspect tick marks and units first.

Pie Chart Analysis.title: 🥧 Pie Chart Analysis — Complete Theory
Pie Chart Analysis.overview: A pie chart divides 360° into sectors. Sector angle is proportional to category value. Convert between percentages, angles, and actual quantities as required.
concepts: Full circle = 360°.
100% corresponds to 360°.
A sector angle is proportional to its percentage or value.
The sum of all sector percentages is 100%.
mistakes: Using 180° instead of 360° for the full circle.
Confusing a sector angle with a percentage.

Line Graph Analysis.title: 📉 Line Graph Analysis — Complete Theory
Line Graph Analysis.overview: Line graphs show how a quantity changes across ordered periods. Focus on trend, absolute change, percentage change, peaks, troughs, and period-to-period differences.
concepts: The x-axis normally represents time or ordered categories.
The y-axis represents the measured quantity.
Upward slope indicates increase; downward slope indicates decrease.
Compare values at the exact periods named in the question.
mistakes: Using the wrong starting period.
Ignoring the y-axis scale.
tips: For percentage change, identify the base period explicitly.

Missing Data Interpretation.title: 🔍 Missing Data Interpretation — Complete Theory
Missing Data Interpretation.overview: Missing-data questions provide constraints such as totals, percentages, averages, ratios, or row/column relationships. The unknown is found by rearranging the constraint.
concepts: If total and other values are known, subtract known values from the total.
If an average is known, multiply average by count to recover total.
If a percentage is known, convert it to a fraction of the total.
Use multiple independent constraints to verify the missing value.
formulas: Missing = Total − Sum of known values
mistakes: Forgetting which values belong to the stated total.
Using percentages as raw numbers.
Failing to check that reconstructed totals match.
tips: Write the governing equation before substituting numbers.
